name: Cowrie shells
what: Small white sea snail shells, mostly the money cowrie Monetaria moneta of the Maldives, used as money from China to West Africa for over a thousand years.
why: The longest-lived currency in history ran on one archipelago's lagoons. In the 18th century European ships carried billions of Maldive shells to West Africa, where they paid for enslaved people.
now: No longer money anywhere, but still used in divination, jewellery and as a symbol of wealth across West Africa and South Asia.

sources.cite: Hogendorn, J. & Johnson, M. (1986). The Shell Money of the Slave Trade. Cambridge University Press.
Yang, B. (2019). Cowrie Shells and Cowrie Money: A Global History. Routledge.
Ibn Battuta, Rihla (c. 1355), trans. H. A. R. Gibb.

stops.note: Women gathered the shells on palm fronds laid in the lagoons, then dried and counted them. Arab writers from the 9th century describe the Maldives' shell trade.
stops.meet: Ibn Battuta, a judge in the Maldives in 1343-1344

stops.note: Shiploads of cowries went to Bengal, where they served as small change for everyday buying until the 19th century; Bengal rice went back to the islands.
In Yunnan cowries were money under the Dali kingdom and long after; Marco Polo saw them there in the 1280s.
stops.meet: Marco Polo, in Yunnan in the 1280s

stops.note: Through the Red Sea and Egypt the shells crossed the Sahara with the caravans.
Ibn Battuta, travelling in Mali in 1352, saw cowries used as money in the markets of the Niger.
The Portuguese shipped cowries home as ballast from the Indian Ocean and on to West Africa.
The VOC bought Maldive shells in Ceylon and Bengal and auctioned them by the ton in Amsterdam to slave traders.

stops.owner: Kingdom of Dahomey and its traders
stops.note: On the Bight of Benin cowries were the money of the Atlantic slave trade: European ships brought billions of shells there in the 18th century. Each shell was a fraction of a person's price; the people sold are the point of this stop.
stops.meet: a person taken from Ouidah's beach to the slave ships

stops.note: From the 1840s traders shipped the larger East African ring cowrie, Monetaria annulus, from Zanzibar by the hundreds of tons.
The flood of East African shells caused one of history's great inflations: cowrie prices in Lagos fell steeply, and under colonial rule shells gave way to coins.
